issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Pregnancy/birth reminders are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner in this 34-year-old male unless there is unreported trauma content involving pregnancy, childbirth, or infants. The other trigger items point toward sexualized/interpersonal threat and hospital-associated reminders, making this item the clearest trauma-incongruent outlier.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Checking Locks: repeatedly check locks, doors, or windows
issues.explanation: Repeated lock-checking is more suggestive of fear of external intrusion/burglary than trauma-specific coping with partner physical abuse, and it is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. The other maladaptive strategies reflect interpersonal avoidance and affect suppression, whereas this item introduces a different safety concern.

issues.item: Threat: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: This threat item duplicates compulsive checking behavior rather than describing a perceived current threat state, and it implies fear of break-in/external danger that is not otherwise supported by the trauma narrative, appraisals, or memory content. In combination with the matching maladaptive strategy item, it forms an internally coherent pair but one that is poorly integrated with the rest of the formulation.

vignette:
Kwame is a 34-year-old parole officer who came to therapy at the urging of his partner, after months of growing withdrawal and a recent incident at work that left him shaken. He is a tall, broad-shouldered man who sits with his arms crossed, his gaze fixed on the floor. He speaks in a low, careful voice, as if every word might cost him something.

The event that changed everything happened two years ago, in the apartment he shared with a man he had been dating for nearly a year. Kwame had come home late from work, exhausted after a day of home visits. They argued about something small-he cannot remember what now. What he remembers is the smell of the antiseptic cleaner his partner had just used on the kitchen counters. He remembers the sound of his own voice rising, then the sound of a hand connecting with his face, then the taste of blood-copper and salt, filling his mouth. He remembers the feeling of the floor against his back, the weight of someone he had trusted pressing down, the hospital smell that came later, in the emergency room, when a nurse dabbed at his split lip with a gauze pad. He remembers thinking, this is not happening, even as it was happening, because it felt like it was still happening, like it would never stop happening. Even now, when the memory returns, it does not feel like a memory. It feels like he is back on that floor, tasting the blood, hearing the thud of his own head against the linoleum.

In the weeks and months that followed, Kwame did not tell anyone at work. He took a few sick days, said he had the flu. He ended the relationship quietly, without explanation. He told himself he would move on, that he would be fine. But he was not fine. He found himself avoiding eye contact with colleagues, especially the men in his office. He started to notice how often men looked at him-on the street, in the grocery store, during meetings-and he began to interpret those looks as threats. A lingering glance from a stranger in a parking lot made his stomach clench. A client who stood too close during a check-in made his breath go shallow. He became certain that other men could see something in him, some weakness, some vulnerability that invited harm. He started scanning every room he entered for exits, for obstacles, for the faces of men who might be watching him too closely.

His body stayed on alert. He could not relax, even at home. His partner would reach for him in bed and he would flinch, then feel ashamed. He began to push away any moment of warmth or pleasure, because those feelings felt dangerous-like letting his guard down, like inviting another blow. He avoided any conversation that might turn into a disagreement. At work, he stopped challenging his parolees when they gave evasive answers. He stopped asking hard questions. He let violations slide, because confronting someone meant conflict, and conflict meant danger. His supervisor noticed. Kwame was put on a performance improvement plan. He told himself he did not care.

What he cared about, what he could not stop thinking about, was the injustice of it all. The man who hurt him was never held accountable. Kwame never filed a police report. He had been too ashamed, too afraid, too convinced that no one would believe him-a man, a parole officer, someone who was supposed to be in control. He had come to believe that his life had been destroyed by what happened, that there was no way back to the person he had been. He started to wonder, in the quiet hours of the night, whether his life was worth living anymore. He did not tell his partner this. He did not tell anyone.

What finally brought him to therapy was a moment at work, three weeks ago. He was in the office break room when a colleague opened a bottle of antiseptic hand sanitizer. The smell hit Kwame like a physical force. He heard the thud again. He tasted the blood. He stood frozen, gripping the counter, the memory so vivid and so present that he lost track of where he was. His supervisor found him there, pale and shaking, and insisted he take leave. His partner made the appointment. Kwame came because he did not know what else to do. He is not sure he wants to be here. He is not sure he wants to feel any of this. But he is tired of being afraid, tired of watching every man who walks past him, tired of a life that feels like it ended two years ago and never started again.
